title: Beef Wellington
subtitle: British beef fillet wrapped in mushroom duxelles and puff pastry
excerpt: Beef Wellington is Britain's most celebrated dinner party centrepiece: a whole fillet of beef coated in a layer of mushroom duxelles and prosciutto, then wrapped in puff pastry and baked until the pastry is golden and the beef is pink. It is a showpiece dish that requires care and timing, but the result is extraordinary.
sourceNotes: The origin of beef Wellington is disputed. The dish may be named after the Duke of Wellington, though there is no evidence he was particularly associated with it. The dish became famous in Britain in the 1960s and 1970s and is now the classic British celebration centrepiece. The combination of beef, mushrooms, and pastry is earlier -- versions of the dish appear in 19th century French cooking as filet de boeuf en croûte.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The Wellington can be assembled up to 24 hours ahead and kept refrigerated. Bake from cold, adding 5 minutes extra.
recipe.temperatureNote: Reduce to 200C after the initial sear period

content.text: The duxelles must be completely dry -- any moisture makes the pastry soggy. Cook the mushrooms until all the liquid has evaporated and the mixture is a dark, dry paste. The beef must be well seared and then chilled before wrapping. A hot centre causes the pastry to cook unevenly. Use a meat thermometer: 52C is rare, 57C is medium-rare.

items.prepNote: all-butter, rolled out to a large rectangle
blitzed to a paste in a food processor

content.text: Make the duxelles: cook {{shallots}} shallots and {{garlic}} garlic in {{unsalted-butter}} butter over medium heat for 3 minutes. Add mushroom paste and {{thyme-fresh}} thyme. Cook over high heat, stirring often, for 12 to 15 minutes until completely dry. Season. Cool completely.

Season {{beef-fillet}} beef with {{salt-table}} salt and {{black-pepper}} pepper. Heat {{vegetable-oil}} oil over very high heat. Sear the beef for 1 to 2 minutes on all sides until brown all over. Cool. Brush all over with {{dijon-mustard}} Dijon mustard. Refrigerate for 20 minutes.

Lay {{prosciutto}} prosciutto slices overlapping on cling film. Spread the duxelles over. Place the beef at the near edge and roll tightly using the cling film. Twist the ends to tighten into a cylinder. Refrigerate for 30 minutes.

Unwrap and place the beef roll on {{puff-pastry}} pastry. Wrap tightly, tucking the ends under. Brush with {{eggs}} beaten egg. Score the top with a knife. Refrigerate for 15 minutes. Preheat oven to 220C. Bake for 25 to 30 minutes until golden (internal temperature 52C for rare, 57C for medium-rare). Rest for 10 minutes before slicing.

items.symptom: The bottom of the pastry is soggy
items.cause: The duxelles was not dry enough, or the beef was not chilled before wrapping.
items.fix: Make the duxelles well ahead and cook it until there is absolutely no moisture left -- it should be a very dark, almost crumbly paste. Chill the beef and the assembled Wellington thoroughly before baking. Bake on a rack so heat circulates under the pastry.

content.text: Beef Wellington is the prestige centrepiece of British dinner party cooking. It became fashionable in the 1960s and has remained the celebration dish of choice in British homes ever since. It appears on restaurant menus across Britain and is the dish most associated with special occasions -- Christmas, New Year, and anniversaries. Gordon Ramsay's version, made famous on television, reintroduced the dish to a new generation.
